title: Yunus, again
hook: he would have stayed in the whale till the Day, had he not glorified Allah (37:143–144)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ranks, angels in rows, and people copying them in prayer. Your line was in ranks.

What if Yunus had never come out of the fish? Surah As-Saffat has a sentence about exactly that. It tells his story again, briefly: the prophet who left in anger, the ship, the lots, the great fish. This path met him back in year one, with the three darknesses and the prayer he cried out from inside. But As-Saffat slips in a sentence found only here. An if. If one thing about Yunus had been different, the story wouldn't have ended on a beach under a gourd vine. It wouldn't have ended at all.

As-Saffat gives the story in ten verses. Yunus was one of the messengers. He fled to the laden ship. Lots were drawn, and he lost. The fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy. Then verses one forty-three and forty-four. Pickthall: "And had he not been one of those who glorify (Allah) He would have tarried in its belly till the day when they are raised". That's the if. The Arabic is mina'l-musabbihin, one of those who glorify, from the same root as subhanallah. Commentators read this two ways, and both are worth keeping. Some say it means his glorifying inside the fish, the cry from year one: there's no god but You, glory to You, I was one of the wrongdoers. Others, reported from early commentators, say it means the glorifying he'd done for years before the fish: prayer and remembrance in easy times, remembered for him in the hard one. A hadith sounds the same note. The Prophet ﷺ told the young Ibn 'Abbas: know Allah in times of ease, and He will know you in times of hardship. On that second reading, the if isn't only about the right words at the worst moment. It's about years of glorifying that came before the dark. The week ran on the same thread: the man from the city's edge ran without waiting, the sun and moon keep a measure set long before, and the rows close up because people have practiced lining up.
screen: `IN THE FISH, OR LONG BEFORE IT?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small tight spot from this week, a deadline, an argument, a worry, and feel where it sits in your body. If you're Muslim, or want to try, say subhanallah, glory be to Allah, quietly, a few times while you hold it; if not, simply name the tight spot and breathe slowly beside it. Starting while things are calm is the point, so the habit is there later.
Yunus. The prophet in the fish, who, As-Saffat says, would have stayed there until the Day of Rising if he hadn't been one who glorifies Allah. Today's word.
Your line: glorifying got him out. In ease first, then in the dark. Another week, done.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the prayer of Yunus (la ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu mina z-zalimin) in times of distress, and make tasbih (subhanallah) part of daily remembrance after each prayer.

what a scholar hears: 37:143–144's conditional is read by some as his tasbih in the fish (21:87) and by others as his earlier worship; the Ibn 'Abbas hadith 'know Allah in ease' is often cited alongside.

chat.says: What does As-Saffat say saved Yunus from staying inside the fish?
options: That he was one of those who glorify God, in the fish or in years before.
That the sailors prayed for him once they had thrown him overboard.
That he promised to go back and finish preaching, so he was released.
chat.meaning: As-Saffat 37:143–144: had he not been one of those who glorify, he'd have stayed in its belly. Commentators read that as in the fish, or before.
